title: Inheritance and abstract classes

notes: Enemy is abstract: you can't write new Enemy(...), only new Goblin(...).
Health has a protected setter: children may change it, outside code can't.
: base(name, 30) runs the parent constructor with the goblin's numbers.
Golem overrides TakeDamage but still calls base.TakeDamage, so the 'never below 0' rule stays in one place.
Golem is sealed: nothing can inherit from it.

exercises.title: An enemy family
exercises.prompt:
The abstract class Enemy is given. Write three kinds of enemy:
- Goblin(string name): 30 HP, AttackDamage() returns 5.
- Troll(string name): 80 HP, AttackDamage() returns 12. Override TakeDamage so a troll only takes half (amount / 2, whole numbers), by calling base.TakeDamage.
- sealed class DragonBoss with a constructor that takes nothing: name "Dragon", 200 HP. AttackDamage() is 25, or 40 once Health is 100 or less. Describe() adds " [BOSS]" to the normal description.

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var t = new Troll("Grum"); t.TakeDamage(21); return t.Describe() + " " + t.AttackDamage(); }))()
tests.name: troll takes half

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var d = new DragonBoss(); int a = d.AttackDamage(); d.TakeDamage(100); return a + " " + d.AttackDamage() + " " + d.Describe(); }))()
tests.name: the dragon gets angry

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { Enemy e = new Troll("T"); e.TakeDamage(1000); return e.Health + " " + e.IsDead; }))()
tests.name: override works through an Enemy variable

tests.why: The troll should reuse the parent's rule with base.TakeDamage(...).

hints: public class Goblin : Enemy { public Goblin(string name) : base(name, 30) { } public override int AttackDamage() => 5; }
Troll: public override void TakeDamage(int amount) => base.TakeDamage(amount / 2);
DragonBoss: public DragonBoss() : base("Dragon", 200) { } and public override string Describe() => base.Describe() + " [BOSS]";

exercises.title: Tower defence turrets
exercises.prompt:
Write the whole family yourself:
- abstract class Turret: Name (get only), Level (get; private set; starts at 1), a protected constructor Turret(string name),
  an abstract int Damage { get; }, a virtual int UpgradeCost => Level * 100, void Upgrade() that adds 1 to Level but throws InvalidOperationException if Level is already 5,
  and ToString() like "Arrow L1: 5 dmg".
- ArrowTurret(): name "Arrow", Damage is 5 * Level.
- CannonTurret(): name "Cannon", Damage is 20 + 10 * (Level - 1), and it overrides UpgradeCost to Level * 150.

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var c = new CannonTurret(); int cost = c.UpgradeCost; c.Upgrade(); return cost + " " + c + " " + c.UpgradeCost; }))()
tests.name: cannon upgrade

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { Turret t = new ArrowTurret(); t.Upgrade(); t.Upgrade(); return t.Damage + " " + t.UpgradeCost; }))()
tests.name: through a Turret variable

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var t = new ArrowTurret(); for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) t.Upgrade(); return "no error"; }))()
tests.name: level 5 is the max

tests.why: The turrets should call the parent constructor with : base("Arrow").

hints: public abstract class Turret { protected Turret(string name) { Name = name; } public abstract int Damage { get; } ... }
public virtual int UpgradeCost => Level * 100; and in CannonTurret: public override int UpgradeCost => Level * 150;
public ArrowTurret() : base("Arrow") { } public override int Damage => 5 * Level;

exercises.title: Composition: a Health component
exercises.prompt:
Instead of a shared parent, give things a Health component.
- Finish class Health: Max and Current (Current starts at Max; constructor throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException if max is 0 or less),
  IsEmpty (true at 0), Damage(int amount) (never below 0; negative amounts do nothing), Heal(int amount) (never above Max; negative amounts do nothing).
- class Player: constructor Player(string name, int maxHealth), Name, and a get-only property Health of type Health.
- class Barrel: a get-only Health property with Max 20, and a bool Explodes that is true when its health is empty.
Player and Barrel must NOT inherit from Health.

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var p = new Player("Amina", 100); p.Health.Damage(30); p.Health.Heal(10); return p.Name + " " + p.Health.Current + "/" + p.Health.Max; }))()
tests.name: a player has health

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var b = new Barrel(); b.Health.Damage(25); return b.Health.Current + " " + b.Explodes; }))()
tests.name: a barrel has health too

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var h = new Health(50); h.Damage(-10); h.Heal(500); return h.Current.ToString(); }))()
tests.name: negative damage and over-healing

tests.why: Player and Barrel should HAVE a Health, not inherit from it.

hints: Health.Damage: Current = Math.Max(0, Current - Math.Max(0, amount));
public class Player { public string Name { get; } public Health Health { get; } public Player(string name, int maxHealth) { Name = name; Health = new Health(maxHealth); } }
public class Barrel { public Health Health { get; } = new Health(20); public bool Explodes => Health.IsEmpty; }

quiz.q: What does `abstract` on a class mean?
choices: You can't create it directly, only its children
quiz.why: Abstract classes are made to be inherited.

quiz.q: A Troll overrides TakeDamage. Why call base.TakeDamage(amount / 2) instead of writing the subtraction again?
choices: The shared rule (never below 0) stays in one place

quiz.q: Which word lets child classes change Health but hides it from everyone else?
quiz.why: protected = this class and its children.

quiz.q: Players and barrels both need health. Best design?
choices: Both inherit from a Health class

quiz.q: Enemy e = new Troll("T"); e.TakeDamage(10); Which TakeDamage runs?
quiz.why: The real object's override runs, whatever the variable's type.

cards.a: virtual has a body children may replace; abstract has none and children must write it

explain: Explain when you'd use inheritance and when you'd use composition, with an example from a game you'd like to make.
